newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian repo pacts seem to have survived first test.
newsitem.headline: Asian repo pacts seem to have survived first test.

text.p: The first real test of a series of agreements between Asian central banks to help each other defend their respective currencies appears to have been successful, economists and traders said on Thursday.
"The symbolic importance (of the central banks' intervention) should not be understated. It's hugely significant," Desmond Supple, a senior analyst at BZW in Singapore, told Reuters.
The Thai baht has been battered by huge sell orders in the last two days from investors and speculators concerned over the future direction of the economy and the currency.
But on Wednesday afternoon, the Bank of Thailand (BOT) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, confirmed they had intervened to defend the baht.

Foreign exchange traders reported that other Asian central banks such as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had also intervened to defend the baht. But apart from the MAS, confirmation from other central banks was not forthcoming.
In the last 18 months, central banks in Asia have been signing up reciprocal repurchase agreements between each other.

The 'repo pacts' give participants instant access to cash for use to defend their currencies. Under the pacts the central bank receiving the assistance will put up U.S. Treasury securities as collateral.
"One's always wondered if these pacts actually mean anything. After yesterday I rather think they do," said the head of Treasury at a European bank in Singapore.

He said the intervention amounts concerned were not necessarily the major factor. "The fact, that of all people, the MAS was prepared to ... be identified with intervention is crucial. They're being seen helping someone out," he said.
The Treasury head also noted the Bank of Japan had said it would be prepared to intervene in the financial markets to help support the baht if it were asked to by the Thai authorities.
"The agreement is there, although it is not a thing we would activate unless we were asked by Thailand," a Bank of Japan (BoJ) official told Reuters.
"Here we've got the BoJ saying they'll defend the baht. Okay it's not with their own money, but when you've got the BoJ on your side is that helpful or not?" the Treasury head said.
BZW's Supple noted that even after news of the MAS's and the BOT's intervention had hit the market, some participants had continued to sell the baht.
But he added, "The market should realise they're not just taking on the Bank of Thailand."
Said the Treasury head; "Thailand's got over US$30 billion in its warchest. Under the repo agreements there's maybe another US$300-400 billion spare (cash) floating around."

He added; "These (repo) agreements make a difference. If the fundamentals are wrong, then fine, kick the hell out of the market. But if you're punting (speculating) then you have to accept you're taking on other central banks."
